lead: Both readings ask who is served by what we do. The Letter to the Ephesians enters an ancient household, with its children and fathers, slaves and masters, and tells each of them to act “as to the Lord”. In Mark, Jesus asks who the Messiah really is, and then warns against religious men who use their office for honour and profit, even at the cost of widows. On the day of Blessed Rani Maria, a sister who spent her life among the poor, the contrast is easy to see.

set: This passage is the end of a “household code” that began at 5:21 with the words “Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ”. Similar lists are found in Colossians 3:18–4:1 and 1 Peter 2:18–3:7, and ancient moral writers discussed the household in much the same way. What is new is the Lord in the midst of it, and the fact that duties run in both directions. Children and slaves are addressed directly, as members of the Church.

The letter is received in the Church as from Paul, writing from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think that a disciple wrote it in his name, while others defend Paul’s authorship. In either case the Church reads it as inspired Scripture.
str: vv. 1–3: children: obedience and the commandment with a promise.
v. 4: fathers: no provocation; formation in the Lord.
vv. 5–8: slaves: service from the heart, as to Christ.
v. 9: masters: the same to them; one Master over both.
kw: Roman law gave a father very great power over his household. Paul’s word to fathers places a limit on that power, and takes the child’s heart seriously.
Formation by training and by the spoken word. The phrase “of the Lord” says what kind of formation it is, and whose.
Literally, receiving the face: judging by a person’s outward position. The Malayalam POC’s മുഖംനോട്ടം catches this exactly. God does not look at rank.
vv: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
“In the Lord” sets both the ground of this obedience and its limit. The next verse quotes the commandment on honouring father and mother (Exodus 20:12).
And, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
A single verse for the father’s whole task: not to crush, and to form. Children often learn who God is from how their parents treat them.
Render service with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not to men and women,
This phrase has given dignity to all sorts of hidden work. It does not bless the condition of slavery; it says that no human being finally owns another person’s service.
for you know that both of you have the same Master in heaven, and with him there is no partiality.
In the ancient world this was a startling thing to say to a slave owner, and it carried a force that later generations would at last draw out.
ch: The Catechism sets out the duties of children (CCC 2214–2220) and of parents (CCC 2221–2231): by obeying the Father themselves, parents teach their children to keep God’s law, and they are the first educators of their children (CCC 2222–2223). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, urges parents to raise their child as an athlete for Christ (Homilies on Ephesians 21; in substance).

set: The questions have ended (12:34), and now Jesus asks one himself, in the Temple. Many of his people expected a Messiah from David’s line, according to God’s promise (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus does not deny this. He asks whether “son of David” says enough. He uses Psalm 110, which was attributed to David, as the people of his time read it. Then he speaks to the crowd about their teachers. Right after this reading comes the poor widow who gives all she has (12:41–44).
str: vv. 35–37a: the Messiah: David’s son and David’s Lord.
v. 37b: the crowd listens with delight.
vv. 38–39: what certain scribes love: robes, greetings, seats.
v. 40: what they do: widows’ houses and long prayers.
kw: In the Greek of the psalm the same word stands for both: “The Lord said to my Lord”. The Hebrew uses God’s name first, then ’ādôn, a word for a master or a king. The early Christians heard in this the risen Jesus, seated at God’s right hand.
Dignified garments that made a teacher noticed. The problem is not the clothing but the love of being seen in it.

Many scholars think of teachers who took advantage of the trust of widows, for example in managing their property. The Law had a special care for widows (Deuteronomy 24:17), which is why this offence is so grave.
vv: David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son?
Jesus leaves the riddle open. A Christian knows the answer: son of David according to the flesh, and Son of God raised in power (Romans 1:3–4).
Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes,

Mark has just shown a scribe who is not far from the kingdom (12:34), so this is no blanket judgement on a whole group. The warning goes to every holder of religious office in any age, and it applies first of all to our own clergy, catechists and parish leaders.
They devour widows’ houses and for the sake of appearance say long prayers.
Prayer used as a screen is, for Jesus, among the worst of abuses. Even a fast can be kept for appearance (Matthew 6:16).
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus claims the title of Lord in a veiled way when he raises Psalm 110 here (CCC 447). The verse “Sit at my right hand” became one of the texts most often quoted in the New Testament, and the Creed echoes it in every Holy Qurbana. Pastors are reminded that authority in the Church is service (CCC 876).

qa: The letter speaks inside a world where slavery was taken for granted, and tiny communities had no power to change the law. It does not attack the institution. It does plant what would one day undo it: one Master over both, no partiality, and in another letter a slave received as “a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). St Gregory of Nyssa was already condemning the owning of human beings in the fourth century (Homilies on Ecclesiastes 4; in substance). The Church now teaches plainly that enslaving human beings is gravely wrong (Gaudium et Spes 27; CCC 2414). This text must never be used to defend it.
rite: Today the Syro-Malabar Church remembers Blessed Rani Maria Vattalil, a Franciscan Clarist sister from Pulluvazhy, who worked among poor tribal families around Udainagar in the diocese of Indore. She helped them to learn, to save, and to stand up to the debts that held them down. On 25 February 1995 she was stabbed to death on a journey by bus, killed by a man hired by those who were losing from her work. Today’s Gospel warns against those who devour the houses of the poor; her life defended them. And what followed is a lesson for the Great Fast: her family forgave the man, who had repented in prison. Her sister visited him and received him as a brother, and her parents welcomed him to their home. She was beatified at Indore on 4 November 2017.
study: Whose service in my home or work do I accept without noticing? How can I thank that person, and how can my own work be done “as to the Lord”?
Where might I enjoy being seen as religious more than I enjoy serving? What would Blessed Rani Maria’s example ask of me?
